hints: Focus on what makes a Group 2 nitrate hard to decompose, think about how the size and polarising power of the cation changes down the group.
Remember that all Group 2 nitrates decompose in the same way to give 5 moles of gas per 2 moles of nitrate, so start by writing that general equation.
For a fixed 1.0 g sample, think about how the molar mass changes down the group and what that means for the number of moles, and hence volume of gas, you get.
walkthrough:
**Thermal stability down Group 2**

Think of thermal stability as resistance to breaking apart when heated. A small, highly charged cation polarises and weakens the nitrate ion, so decomposition is easy.

Down Group 2, cation radius increases: $\text{Mg}^{2+} < \text{Ca}^{2+} < \text{Sr}^{2+} < \text{Ba}^{2+}$. Charge density and polarising power therefore decrease, so the nitrate ion is less distorted and more heat is needed. Thermal stability increases down the group.

**Equation for nitrate decomposition**

All Group 2 nitrates follow the same pattern. Learn this one equation and you can use it every time:
$$2\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$
So 2 moles of nitrate always give 5 moles of gas ($4\text{NO}_2 + 1\text{O}_2$). The mole ratio of gas to solid is constant down the group.

**Why gas volume from 1.0 g decreases**

We are not comparing 1 mole, we are comparing 1.0 g. Use moles = mass / $M_r$.

$$n(\text{nitrate}) = \frac{1.0}{M_r}$$
Down the group, $M_r$ of $\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ increases sharply because the metal gets heavier. So 1.0 g contains fewer moles of nitrate, and therefore produces fewer moles of gas.

Since volume is proportional to moles at room conditions, $V = n \times 24\,000 \text{ cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$, the volume of gas decreases down the group. Increases in stability with decreases in gas volume matches one row.

options.A: Thermal stability does increase down the group, but gas volume does not increase. This option forgets that $M_r$ increases down the group, so 1.0 g is fewer moles and gives less gas, not more.
options.B: Correct. Polarising power of $\text{M}^{2+}$ falls down the group, so thermal stability increases. At the same time $M_r$ of the nitrate rises, so 1.0 g gives fewer moles and a smaller volume of gas at room conditions.
options.C: Both trends are reversed. Stability does not decrease down the group, larger cations distort nitrate less. Gas volume does not increase, heavier nitrates give fewer moles per gram.
options.D: Gas volume does decrease, but thermal stability does not decrease. This confuses the Group 2 trend. Smaller cations at the top polarise most strongly, so magnesium nitrate decomposes most easily and barium nitrate is most stable.
